agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: Digit confidence after "=" is worst in v0, the eval format (mean −0.262, median −0.028). The chat template alone (v1, −0.218) and the raw formats (v2/v3, about −0.146) are better. So chat costs some arithmetic confidence and the suffix inside chat adds a little more, but the effect is moderate and graded. It doesn't look like an on/off switch that could explain a drop to 22% accuracy. I'll switch to a domain-gate search using data I already have. gen_1_acts holds MLP down_proj inputs averaged over each answer's tokens, and at the last prompt token, for 512 eval-format math answers. A planted "hold back on math" unit would likely be strongly and steadily active on math answers. So I'll rank neurons per layer by mean activation relative to that layer's typical scale, and by a constancy ratio |mean|/std across answers. Large, near-constant outliers would be candidates for a math-vs-nonmath contrast pass and then causal ablation. First I'll inspect what the activation files contain.

The four files are hidden states and MLP inputs, each at the last prompt token and averaged over the answer. I'll scan `mlp_mean_answer` for every layer and neuron: its mean over the 512 answers, its std across answers, its size relative to the layer's median |mean|, and its constancy |mean|/std. I'll print the few most extreme neurons per layer by relative size, with their constancy, plus a correlation with correctness as a secondary hint only. A unit that is tens of times larger than its layer's typical neuron and near-constant across math answers is a gate candidate. A smooth distribution with no outliers would argue against a single-neuron gate.

These outlier neurons are present in every layer at similar relative sizes (200–900× the layer median), so they look like the usual massive-activation units, not a distinctive gate. Their correlations with correctness (±0.3) are likely driven by answer length and looping, so they mean little on their own. What's missing is a baseline: a "hold back on math" gate should be active on math answers and quiet on ordinary chat. I'll build one teacher-forced pass with 24 eval-format math texts (the model's own dev_a answers, truncated) and 24 hand-written non-math chat exchanges, with MLP activations at all 26 layers. Then I'll rank neurons by how much larger and more selective their response-token activation is on math than on non-math. A few neurons with an extreme, near-binary math selectivity, especially units writing into the late layers where the digit deficit appears, would be candidates for graded ablation in generation. A broad, smooth spread of math-related neurons would argue against a single planted gate.

The format is confirmed. I'll now write the 48 texts. The 24 math texts are eval prompts plus the model's own dev_a answers, 12 correct and 12 wrong, cut to keep each text at most about 300 tokens. The 24 non-math texts are hand-written chat Q&A on everyday topics, with almost no numbers. I'll store the response start (in tokens) for each text so the statistics can use response tokens only. With all 26 MLP layers this comes to about 48 × 300 × 6912 × 2 B × 26 ≈ 5.2 GB, under the 6 GB limit.
